item.title: MST: Lane Pinnacle, 8 miles — Mon Sep 7, 8:30 AM
item.description:
The Asheville Hiking Group Trailhead is Tanbark Tunnel on the BRP. From Tanbark Tunnel, we take the MST spur trail up to Rattlesnake Lodge and then the MST over Rich Knob, Wolf Den, and then up to Lane Pinnacle where we have views of the North Fork Reservoir and its surrounding watershed. Then we turn around and head back down.
Distance out and up is approximately 4 miles (8 miles round trip), and the elevation out and up is approximately 2,000 feet.
**2,000 feet elevation gain is no mean feat**. Most of the gain up to Rich Knob, about 1,700 feet, is in the first 2 miles--gives new meaning to the term "unrelenting." The rest is up and down to Lane Pinnacle. So . . . 2,000 feet up and 2,000 feet down over 8 miles.
**Car pool:** Meet at Folk Art Center, **lower parking level** at 8:30. Limited parking at the trail head.

item.title: Sleepy Gap--Lake Powhatan 8 miles, 1300' — Wed Sep 9, 8:00 AM
item.description: The Asheville Hiking Group Description: Hike from the Blue Ridge Parkway, along the Mountain-to-Sea trail, through Bent Creek and around Lake Powhatan, then back to the BRP. Good footing; mostly wide trails; some nearby creeks; nice view from Sleepy Gap. From Sleepy Gap south on the MST via Chestnut Cove to Explorer and Pine Tree loops. Then circle the Lake and have a snack at the picnic tables. Ascend via Small Creek and Deerfield Connector to the unmarked Stambaugh trail and the MST back to Sleepy Gap. Type: Loop. Max elev: 3200’. Avg moving pace: 2.4 mph. Difficulty (1=effortless, 10=hard): 6. item.title: Long-term Effects of Hurricane Helene on Southern Appalachian Ecosystems — Wed Sep 23, 1:00 PM
item.description:
Long-term Effects of Hurricane Helene on Southern Appalachian Ecosystems with Dan Lazar Wednesday, September 23 | 1 pm – 3 pm BRN – Core | BREG – Elective Register Here!
It has been two years since hurricane Helene ravaged the ecosystems of Western North Carolina, uprooting trees and causing major flooding along mountain rivers and streams. How have the animals and plants of the affected areas responded to this historic event? Where do songbirds go to escape hurricane winds? How can fish and aquatic invertebrates tolerate such massive flooding? What factors determine which trees are toppled and which survive? We will investigate the long-term effects of Hurricane Helene on the natural plant and animal communities of Western North Carolina during this illustrated lecture followed by a short walk on Arboretum grounds to observe the ongoing recovery of hurricane-damaged areas. Dan Lazar served for many years as the director of education at the Western North Carolina Nature

item.description:
Healthy Soil for Healthy Crops with Mark Dempsey Thursday, September 24 | 1 pm – 4 pm BREG – Soil Health Core Register Here!
Come learn about how soil works and how to improve soil health. We will cover the basics of soil, the critical role of organic matter, how to sample soil and interpret a nutrient test, and what actions you can take to make your soil better. Drawing from research and on-farm experience, the class emphasizes practical, science-based strategies for improving soil health, reducing erosion, and building resilient farming systems. Mark Dempsey works with the Carolina Farm Stewardship Association as conservation specialist and soil health educator. His background includes more than 15 years of research and education in soil microbiology, no-till farming, cover crops, and sustainable agriculture systems. He teaches practical, science-based approaches to improving soil health, soil function, and long-term farm resilience.
